strengths: The paper tackles an important problem—training-free video reasoning segmentation—and proposes a coherent pipeline combining contrastive object-background attention, complementary video-frame attention, and attention-guided SAM2 prompting.

The empirical scope is strong: experiments cover five referring/reasoning VOS benchmarks, several MLLM families and model sizes, both coarse attention masks and dense SAM2 masks, and relevant J/F metrics.

Results consistently improve over the evaluated training-free attention baselines, with particularly large gains on reasoning-oriented datasets. The Qwen2.5-VL-7B configuration is competitive with several trained systems on Ref-DAVIS and ReasonVOS.

Ablations separately study contrastive fusion, video-frame fusion, multi-scale processing, rollout normalization, layer choice, prompting thresholds, attention-consistency scoring, and model scaling. These generally provide convincing evidence that the components contribute.

The method is conceptually simple and broadly applicable to attention-based MLLMs, while the qualitative examples cover single-object, multi-object, small-object, temporal-reasoning, and world-knowledge cases.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the system largely combines attention rollout, positive-negative prompt subtraction, video/frame averaging, thresholding, and SAM2 proposal filtering. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its conceptual contribution from a carefully engineered composition of existing techniques.

The baseline set does not establish that attention extraction is the best training-free strategy. A crucial comparison is a two-stage pipeline that asks the same MLLM to infer the target category and then uses an off-the-shelf open-vocabulary grounder or detector with SAM2. Other simple controls, such as object-only attention plus the proposed SAM pipeline, should also be reported more broadly.

Comparisons with Loc-Head are difficult to interpret because the authors alter its model-specific head-selection heuristic and replace its original SAM prompting procedure with their own. This is useful as a component comparison, but it is not a clean evaluation of the published baseline; both the canonical method and controlled hybrids should be reported.

Claims of comparability to training-based methods are somewhat overstated. Many comparisons use different, often newer and stronger, MLLM backbones. Against the Qwen2.5-VL-based Veason-R1, DecAF is close on ReasonVOS but notably behind on ReVOS, so matched-backbone conclusions are mixed.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: the promised code URL is blank, and important implementation details are underspecified, including the exact weighted-head aggregation and normalization equations, decoding settings, input resolutions and frame counts across experiments, SAM2 propagation details, NMS implementation, and computational cost. The multiple video/frame/background forward passes and many SAM2 tracklets may be expensive, but no runtime or memory analysis is provided.

The evaluation reports only aggregate point estimates, without uncertainty, repeated-run sensitivity, per-category breakdowns, or analysis of errors caused by incorrect category prediction. Since contrastive prompting depends critically on the inferred category and MLLM generation, this missing analysis limits confidence in robustness.

There are presentation inconsistencies—most notably “decomposed” versus “decoupled” attention fusion—and the qualitative section mainly shows selected successes. Although several failure cases are included, quantitative stratification by target size, temporal presence, object count, and reasoning type would better substantiate the proposed mechanisms.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: training-free video reasoning segmentation using localization signals already present in multimodal language models.
The proposed pipeline is intuitive and reasonably well motivated, combining object-background contrast, video-frame fusion, vision-weighted attention rollout, and SAM2-based mask refinement.
Evaluation spans five referring/reasoning video segmentation datasets, several MLLM families and model sizes, and both coarse attention masks and dense SAM2 masks.

The reported gains over the authors' Loc-Head reproduction are often substantial, particularly on ReasonVOS, and the component, threshold, layer, and model-scaling ablations provide useful diagnostic evidence.
The manuscript is generally readable and includes qualitative successes as well as several informative failure cases.
weaknesses: The central comparative evidence is not sufficiently fair or controlled. Loc-Head is evaluated using the proposed paper's SAM prompting pipeline rather than its original end-to-end procedure, yet the resulting rows are presented as method-level comparisons. TAM is run under a prompt/protocol that the paper itself says causes it to fail, producing implausibly low scores. These modified baselines do not establish superiority over faithfully implemented prior methods.

ReasonVOS is described as having only a test set and supporting zero-shot evaluation, but that same set is repeatedly used for ablations over fusion choices, rollout layers, scoring rules, and thresholds. This creates test-set selection leakage and weakens the claimed zero-shot results.

The comparison with training-based methods is not well controlled for MLLM backbone, SAM version, input resolution, frame sampling, or computational budget. Consequently, statements that DecAF is comparable or superior to trained systems are stronger than the presented evidence supports.

Important practical baselines are absent, such as prompting an MLLM to produce boxes or points and then using SAM2, and other detector/grounder-plus-SAM2 training-free pipelines. The evaluation therefore does not show that attention rollout is necessary relative to simpler training-free localization strategies.

The method is largely a composition of heuristic operations—prompted attention subtraction, averaging video/frame maps, thresholding, and SAM2 filtering—so the conceptual novelty is moderate. The paper provides limited analysis of why these operations should be reliable beyond empirical ablations.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The promised code URL is blank, while Gaussian smoothing parameters, exact resolutions and frame sampling for dense-mask experiments, weighted-head aggregation details, normalization conventions, SAM2 propagation order, temporal NMS computation, and treatment of missing or duplicated tracklets are underspecified.

The attention-consistency score is not adequately characterized: its range and calibration relative to SAM confidence are unclear, yet the heterogeneous quantities are simply averaged and thresholded. There is no analysis of numerical stability or principled justification for this combination.

The claimed robustness to thresholds is overstated: Table 6 shows meaningful variation, and the best configuration differs by dataset. No validation-only selection protocol, uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or statistical significance analysis is provided.

Some technical exposition is inconsistent or incomplete, including switching between 'Decomposed' and 'Decoupled' Attention Fusion, ambiguous attention-tensor dimensions and head-weight normalization, and an unclear description of how time-indexed point queries are sequentially introduced and propagated by SAM2.

Efficiency is central to the practicality of full attention rollout over video tokens and repeated frame/video MLLM passes, but the paper reports no runtime, memory use, number of forward passes, SAM2 query counts, or comparison of computational cost with competing approaches.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: adapting MLLMs to video reasoning segmentation without task-specific training. The proposed combination of contrastive object-background attention, complementary video-frame fusion, and attention-guided SAM2 prompting is intuitive and practically useful.

The empirical study is broad, covering five referring/reasoning VOS datasets, multiple MLLM families and model sizes, both coarse attention masks and dense SAM2 masks, and several relevant training-free and training-based comparisons.

The results provide concrete positive evidence: DecAF consistently improves over the strongest evaluated training-free baseline on reasoning-oriented datasets, with especially strong performance from Qwen2.5VL-7B. It also approaches some task-trained systems despite requiring no additional optimization.

The ablations separately examine contrastive fusion, video-frame fusion, multi-scale processing, rollout normalization, layer choice, prompting thresholds, and attention-consistency scoring. The sizeable and generally consistent gains support the main design choices.

The method is clearly motivated and presented, and the qualitative examples cover single-object, multi-object, small-object, temporal-reasoning, and world-knowledge cases, alongside informative failure cases.
weaknesses: The novelty is primarily in combining relatively simple prompting, subtraction/averaging, attention-rollout weighting, and SAM2 filtering heuristics. The paper would benefit from more careful positioning of which elements are fundamentally new versus adaptations of existing attention-rollout and attention-as-prompt pipelines.

The baseline comparison is not fully controlled. The authors replace Loc-Head's original SAM prompting with their own pipeline for subsequent comparisons, so the rows labeled Loc-Head do not represent the complete original method and partially inherit the proposed method. Some comparisons also use different MLLM variants, such as LLaVA-7B versus LLaVA-OV-7B.

There is at least one apparent numerical inconsistency: in Table 2, the InternVL3-8B Loc-Head ReasonVOS entry reports J&F=39.6 while J=47.0 and F=43.3, whose mean is approximately 45.2. Such errors reduce confidence in the experimental reporting and should be corrected or explained.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the promised code link is blank, and important operational details such as Gaussian smoothing parameters, exact input resolutions, computational cost, memory requirements, and the number of SAM2 tracklets evaluated are missing. This is particularly relevant because the method requires multiple video/frame MLLM passes and repeated SAM2 propagation.

The protocol for selecting rollout layers and thresholds is insufficiently specified. Table 6 shows dataset-dependent optima, but the paper does not clearly identify a held-out validation protocol or establish that test-set results were not used in design choices. Results also lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis.

The method relies critically on the MLLM predicting the correct object category, yet category-selection accuracy and sensitivity are not evaluated independently. Efficiency and robustness under incorrect categories, ambiguous multi-object expressions, or absent targets also receive limited quantitative analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem and proposes a genuinely training-free pipeline combining MLLM attention rollout with SAM2 for video reasoning segmentation.
The evaluation is broad, covering five datasets, several MLLM families and model sizes, both coarse attention masks and dense SAM2 masks, and referring as well as reasoning-oriented settings.
The reported improvements over training-free baselines are substantial, especially on ReasonVOS, and the paper includes useful comparisons with Qwen2.5-VL native grounding.

Ablations separately examine object-background fusion, video-frame fusion, multi-scale processing, rollout normalization, SAM thresholds, and tracklet scoring. The qualitative examples and acknowledged failure modes further aid interpretation.
The core intuition is simple and compelling: background subtraction suppresses attention sinks, while video-frame fusion combines temporal context with finer spatial evidence.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. Much of the pipeline consists of established attention rollout, subtraction and averaging of maps, thresholding, NMS, and SAM2 propagation. The vision-aware head weighting and consistency score are useful heuristics but receive limited theoretical or diagnostic justification.

The strongest comparisons are not fully controlled. Training-based systems use different MLLMs, segmentation models, input resolutions, and sampling strategies, so claims of surpassing training-based methods—particularly the asserted translation from reasoning ability to localization—are stronger than the evidence supports.

The Loc-Head comparison raises reproducibility and fairness concerns. The authors report failing to reproduce its published RefCOCO result by a very large margin, introduce model-specific changes to its attention-sink heuristic, and replace its SAM prompting procedure with their own. These modified results should not be presented as an unqualified comparison to the published method without stronger validation.

ReasonVOS is described as having only a test set, yet it is repeatedly used for threshold and rollout-layer ablations. Even though the stated default thresholds are not the best test-set configuration, inspecting this sweep undermines the clean zero-shot characterization and creates test-set selection concerns.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including Gaussian smoothing parameters, exact input resolutions, handling and union of multiple retained tracklets, frame-to-full-video propagation details, and the precise ordering of weighted aggregation, residual addition, and normalization in rollout. The displayed tensor dimensions and reused notation for the rollout matrices are also ambiguous.

The method appears computationally expensive: it requires multiple video-level and frame-level MLLM passes, storage or processing of attention matrices across many layers, and potentially many SAM2 propagations. No runtime, memory, number-of-query, or compute comparison is provided, making the practical meaning of “training-free” incomplete.

Robustness is evaluated mainly through prompt paraphrases and selected qualitative examples. There is little quantitative breakdown by object size, video length, target absence, number of instances, or reasoning type, despite these being central to the proposed method and its documented failure cases.

Overall, the empirical signal is promising, but fairer controlled comparisons, a clean validation protocol, efficiency analysis, and more complete reproducibility details are needed for the work to be clearly above the top-tier acceptance threshold.

The experiments cover several MLLM families and five referring/reasoning VOS datasets. The reported improvements over reproduced training-free alternatives are often substantial, especially with Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
The paper includes useful component, threshold, layer, model-size, and prompt-variation studies, as well as a direct Qwen2.5-VL grounding baseline and several acknowledged failure cases.

The attention-guided SAM2 stage is practically motivated: it converts coarse attention into substantially stronger masks and attempts to reject spurious tracklets using an attention-consistency score.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. DecAF mainly combines attention rollout, prompt-conditioned map subtraction, averaging of video/frame maps, thresholding, NMS, and SAM2. These are largely heuristic combinations of established components, and the paper provides little theoretical or diagnostic insight explaining when the method should work.

The evaluation protocol raises a serious test-set-validity concern. ReasonVOS is explicitly described as providing only a test set, yet it is repeatedly used for component ablations, layer selection, threshold sweeps, and design analysis. Calling the resulting evaluation zero-shot is therefore questionable, and repeated test-set feedback weakens the central performance claim.

The baseline comparison is not sufficiently controlled. Loc-Head is substantially modified using model-specific attention-sink rules and then paired with the authors' own SAM prompting procedure; the appendix reports severe reproduction discrepancies from Loc-Head's published results. Consequently, the tables do not cleanly compare complete existing systems under their validated implementations. Comparable native-grounding and simpler prompting baselines are also only evaluated for Qwen2.5-VL on two datasets.

The claim of being training-free obscures potentially high inference cost. DecAF requires multiple video- and frame-level MLLM passes for object and background prompts, higher-resolution frame processing, extraction and rollout of large attention matrices, and potentially many SAM2 tracklets. No runtime, memory, FLOP, number-of-forward-pass, or accuracy-efficiency analysis is provided.

Important implementation details are missing or ambiguous, including the exact weighted-head aggregation equation and normalization, Gaussian smoothing parameters, precise checkpoints and input resolutions, dataset splits, tracklet propagation in both temporal directions, treatment and union of multiple retained objects, and several SAM2/NMS settings. The displayed code-availability statement also lacks an accessible link in the submitted manuscript.

Several broad conclusions exceed the evidence. Attention correlation does not establish that an MLLM's reasoning directly causes localization; answer/category correctness is not analyzed, and possible benchmark exposure of pretrained MLLMs is not considered. The assertion that the method is modality-agnostic and extendable beyond vision is entirely unevaluated.

Multi-object and fine-grained claims remain weakly supported. The category-selection prompt requests a single label, the multiple-object study uses a manually extracted subset with no selection protocol, and part-level behavior is shown only through selected qualitative examples where SAM2 sometimes fails.

The paper contains terminology and presentation inconsistencies, such as alternating between 'Decomposed' and 'Decoupled' Attention Fusion. More importantly, no uncertainty estimates, repeated-run analysis, or statistical testing are reported despite conclusions being drawn from relatively small benchmark differences in several settings.

strengths: DecAF offers a clear and practically useful contribution: it adapts pretrained MLLMs and SAM2 to video reasoning segmentation without task-specific training.

The evaluation is broad, covering five referring/reasoning VOS benchmarks, three MLLM families, and multiple model sizes. Gains over the closest training-free baselines are generally substantial, especially on reasoning-oriented datasets.

The component studies support the proposed design: object-background contrast, video-frame fusion, vision-aware rollout, multi-scale processing, and attention-consistency scoring each provide measurable benefits.
The paper includes useful robustness analyses for prompts and thresholds, a native Qwen2.5-VL grounding baseline, multi-object and part-level analyses, and qualitative failure cases.

The method is conceptually simple, well motivated, and relevant: it exposes useful localization signals already present in video MLLMs and turns them into competitive masks using a training-free pipeline.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The main operations—positive/negative attention subtraction, averaging video- and frame-level maps, and filtering SAM2 proposals—are intuitive combinations of existing attention-rollout and segmentation techniques rather than a major methodological advance.

Baseline fairness is not fully clean. Dense-mask results for Loc-Head use the authors' SAM2 prompting procedure because the original procedure reproduces poorly; although this isolates attention quality, it is not a direct comparison to the published end-to-end baseline. Several Loc-Head heuristics are also modified per architecture.

The strongest results combine several advantages beyond attention fusion, including higher-resolution frame processing and a bespoke SAM2 proposal, propagation, NMS, and tracklet-scoring pipeline. The ablations are helpful, but attribution would be stronger with comparisons against standard SAM2 prompting alternatives under matched resolution and computation.

ReasonVOS is described as test-only and zero-shot, yet it is repeatedly used in threshold, rollout-layer, and design ablations. This creates a risk of test-set-informed method selection and weakens the zero-shot interpretation unless all choices were fixed using separate development data.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript omits or leaves ambiguous some consequential details such as Gaussian smoothing parameters, exact input resolutions and tiling settings, decoding settings, definitive NMS configuration, computational cost, and runtime/memory. The displayed code-availability statement also lacks a usable link.

The paper does not report uncertainty, repeated runs, or significance testing. It also emphasizes comparisons with trained systems whose backbones, sampling, and training resources differ, so claims of matching or surpassing training-based methods should be qualified.

Attention rollout is treated as token influence with limited discussion of its known limitations as an explanation mechanism. Moreover, performance depends on the MLLM first identifying the correct object category, but category-prediction accuracy and its downstream error contribution are not quantified.
